name: Tiered sensing architecture and surveillance cadence
consequences: Maintains nightly low-burden monitoring across 8 active suites with scheduled enhanced PSG nights on the first, mid-stay, and final nights; the downstream effect is stronger data resolution on targeted nights and preserved safety margins. If escalation nights are not sufficiently frequent or well-aligned with events, there is a risk of missed infrequent episodes, increasing downstream annotation workload to resolve false positives.
options: Maintain nightly low-burden monitoring with dry-electrode EEG headbands and contact-free sensors across 8 active suites, reserving enhanced PSG nights for mid-stay and final observations to preserve data quality.
Expand low-burden monitoring to all nights with continuous ambient sensing and infrared review, reducing dependence on plan-driven escalation while preserving safety buffers.
Implement a semi-automated event-triage trigger to escalate to full PSG only after technician-flagged events, balancing data resolution with staff workload and annotation throughput.
review: Trade-off is that maintaining a tiered strategy supports safety and data depth but risks missing infrequent events if escalation cadence is not optimized; the three options do not guarantee uniform detection across all nights.

name: Data governance and privacy boundaries
consequences: Safeguards participant privacy by restricting bedroom video from public repositories and depositing only de-identified physiological datasets under data-use agreements. Downstream, these privacy protections constrain external replication and validation, potentially slowing cross-site benchmarking.
options: Maintain strict data controls by depositing only de-identified sensor data into recognized repositories under strict data-use agreements and excluding bedroom video from public access.
Establish a tiered access framework granting researchers controlled, on-site data exploration with approved non-disclosive outputs while protecting participant privacy.
Form a data governance board to codify release criteria, audit sharing requests, and coordinate with University of Bonn and funders to avoid ad hoc disclosures.
review: Privacy versus openness is the primary trade-off; the options do not uniformly address how to share video-derived metrics or enable cross-institution benchmarking within ethical constraints.

name: Recruitment strategy reinforcement
consequences: Targets 50–70 participants through the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologists, and the DGFSSN network; downstream, if recruitment lags, the program risks failing to meet event capture targets required for Aim 2 and publications.
options: Maintain current recruitment channels to target 50–70 participants and adhere to strict inclusion/exclusion criteria to preserve study integrity.
Balance recruitment by expanding local referrals and outreach within Bonn to accelerate enrollment while upholding safety screens.
Implement a structured pre-admission pathway with collateral histories and prior PSG review to pre-select high-probability event yield participants.
review: Strict screening preserves data quality but reduces the eligible pool; the options do not specify retention strategies for participants during uncertain stays.

name: Expansion readiness and capacity planning
consequences: Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until pilot demonstrates data quality, acceptable false alarm rates, safe staffing, and annotation throughput; proceeding earlier could strain safety and data integrity.
options: Proceed with phased expansion to 12 suites only after pilot demonstrates data quality, acceptable false alarm rates, safe staffing, and annotation throughput.
Pursue parallel expansion in a separate facility while maintaining current 8-suite operations to test normalization.
Adopt modular retrofits and flexible space planning to allow scalable growth within the existing property while preserving domestic feel.
review: Ramping capacity is risk-managed but creates schedule pressure; the options do not specify funding milestones or contingency plans for delayed expansion.

name: Staffing model and night coverage
consequences: Three rotating night technicians cover 8 active suites and maintain safety margins; expansion to 12 suites would require more staff and could slow expansion.
options: Maintain current trio of rotating night technicians to cover 8 suites with a margin for events, preserving safety without overextending staffing.
Develop a cross-trained on-call pool to supplement nightly coverage during peak events and minimize response delays.
Implement formal escalation timelines and protocols to guide rapid response in event-triggered scenarios while ensuring staff wellbeing.
review: Fixed staffing supports safety but constrains growth; the options do not specify cost or recruitment timelines for expanding beyond 8 suites.

name: Annotation reliability and dual-scorer workflow
consequences: Two independent scorers using AASM criteria ensures reliability, but doubles manual workload and can slow processing of nights during high throughput.
options: Sustain real-time night technician annotations and two independent scorers to maintain high reliability and auditability across all monitored nights.
Introduce a periodic external audit of 10% of nights to validate internal scoring without overburdening the core team.
Establish structured adjudication meetings for discordant events to streamline resolution and reduce backlog of remaining nights.
review: Reliability versus throughput is the core trade-off; the options do not specify how to accelerate adjudication or introduce semi-automation within ethical constraints.

name: Semi-automated event-triage with human-in-the-loop
consequences: Shifting toward semi-automated event triage reduces the manual review burden by prioritizing clear nocturnal events for rapid human scoring. The approach increases dependence on algorithmic classification, which may bias detection of subtle parasomnia patterns and requires ongoing calibration across nights.
options: Implement a semi-automated event triage algorithm that flags high-likelihood parasomnia events for rapid human review, reducing reviewer workload while maintaining scoring accuracy.
Maintain exclusive human scoring with expanded reviewer hours and staggered night shifts to manage annotation throughput without relying on automation.
Deploy a hybrid triage protocol that first screens all data with a lightweight heuristic, then routes uncertain cases to both scorers for consensus.
review: Trade-off is automation risk of misclassifying subtle events against the reliability of human review; the gap is whether the three options ensure consistent detection across all nights and event types without introducing backlog.

name: Recruitment channel diversification strategy
consequences: Broadening recruitment channels increases enrollment potential and diversifies participant characteristics, supporting Aim 1 and Aim 2 evidence richness. However, it adds screening workload, logistics, and potential cross-site variability that complicates baseline comparisons.
options: Formalize feeder clinics and bed partner networks to funnel eligible participants, expanding eligibility capture while maintaining safety oversight.
Rely primarily on University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic referrals to preserve control and minimize variability in pre-screening.
Launch regional outreach with patient advocacy groups and regional neurologists to broaden access, while implementing standardized pre-screening checklists.
review: Trade-off is broader access versus higher screening burden and cross-site variability; the gap is whether standardized pre-screening can align all new channels to a common eligibility threshold.

name: Expansion gating based on data quality thresholds
consequences: Linking expansion to data quality milestones aligns growth with demonstrated performance, reducing the risk of overextension. A slower scale is possible if achieving reliable inter-rater consistency and sufficient event yield proves difficult, leaving capacity underutilized until criteria are met.
options: Establish quantitative data quality milestones to trigger facility expansion only after achieving consistent inter-rater reliability and event yield.
Proceed with facility expansion plans irrespective of data quality to capitalize on timelines, accepting increased risk of underpowered results.
Adopt a rolling data quality dashboard that guides incremental expansion while maintaining current occupancy limits.
review: Trade-off favors caution over speed; the gap is whether the chosen quality milestones fully capture the nuances needed to justify scaling, given recruitment and annotation throughput dynamics.

name: Privacy-preserving data-sharing posture
consequences: Implementing privacy-first data sharing defines access controls and reduces risk, potentially expediting publications within approved channels. However, external validation and multi-institution replication may be impeded by restricted video data and controlled data releases.
options: Publish de-identified physiological and sensor datasets to recognized repositories with formal data use agreements, balancing openness against privacy constraints.
Maintain strict non-public sharing and internal use for all video data, while sharing aggregated statistics to collaborators.
Implement tiered access with controlled release of de-identified data plus a data access review panel to maintain privacy and utility.
review: Trade-off is privacy versus openness; the gap is how to balance rigorous external validation and collaboration with strict privacy controls across data streams.

name: Environment design leverage for naturalistic data
consequences: Adjusting the residential environment affects ecological validity and safety; a more naturalistic layout reduces participant stress and may improve authentic parasomnia patterns, but increases environmental noise and inconsistent event capture. Conversely, a more clinical setup can improve control yet risks suppressing natural behavior. Finding the balance is essential to maintain comparability with real-world conditions.
options: Optimize residential layout and sensory attenuation to minimize participant stress while preserving naturalistic nocturnal behavior for high-quality data.
Intensify clinical ambiance with more monitoring and safety features to maximize protocol compliance but risk altering participant behavior.
Adjust room-by-room variations to test environment effects on parasomnia expression while maintaining safety and privacy.
review: Trade-off is realism versus control; the gap is whether the three options provide a repeatable environmental protocol that yields comparable event rates across nights and rooms.

name: Inter-rater reliability optimization framework
consequences: Strengthening scoring consistency reduces misclassification risk and supports robust phenotyping, which strengthens Aim 2 outputs. However, it may slow data processing and extend turnaround times if extensive calibration is required.
options: Institute structured adjudication rounds with concordance scoring and feedback to standardize scoring criteria across raters.
Provide comprehensive rater calibration sessions using annotated gold-standard datasets to strengthen consistency without burdening workflow.
Adopt a consensus review protocol where ambiguous events are discussed in bi-weekly meetings to reach agreement.
review: Trade-off is higher accuracy versus throughput; the gap is whether the workflow scales with increasing event volume and partner sites.

name: Phased capacity scaling tied to data quality milestones
consequences: Expanding from 8 active suites toward 12 will only occur after the pilot demonstrates acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. This creates a clear go/no-go path but postpones enrollment acceleration and could slow publications if milestones lag.
options: Limit expansion to 8 active suites while implementing milestone-driven hiring and training programs to sustain safety margins during the pilot phase.
Advance to 12 suites in a staged rollout only after achieving predefined data quality and annotation-throughput metrics across the pilot cohort.
Preserve 8 suites but reallocate space to expand enhanced-night PSG on peak weeks to increase data yield without expanding staffing complexity.
review: Trade-off: expanding capacity accelerates data collection but adds staffing and safety overhead; the gap is that milestones may not capture data quality plateaus or the need for external partnerships to maintain momentum.

name: Naturalistic environment fidelity and safety controls balance
consequences: The environment design must maintain domestic feel to elicit naturalistic behavior, but safety protocols must remain robust; overly clinical cues risk suppressing naturalistic responses. If fidelity is pushed too far in one direction, safety overhead or intrusion into participants' routines may rise, harming comfort and data quality.
options: Maintain domestic-feel spaces with discreet safety features, ensuring observation remains non-intrusive while preserving rapid response capability.
Reconfigure areas to simulate home environment more closely while upgrading padding, silent alarms, and escape-proof layouts to reduce intrusion and maintain safety.
Prioritize clinician-visible clinical safety tests and privacy-preserving camera placements to strengthen safety without undermining naturalistic behavior.
review: Trade-off: fidelity enhancements may degrade throughput if safety checks slow monitoring; gap: lacks a quantitative plan to measure naturalistic engagement across configurations.

name: Data storage and transfer governance for synchronized streams
consequences: Data streams are time-synchronized, stored on a local NAS, and backed up nightly to university storage with de-identification and privacy controls; expanding cross-site access increases resilience but adds governance overhead and potential latency for scoring.
options: Maintain local NAS-first storage with automatic nightly encrypted backups to university storage, ensuring rapid access for scoring and strict regulatory compliance.
Implement modular data handoff with tiered access control and audit trails to support cross-site collaboration while preserving privacy constraints.
Introduce edge preprocessing to compress and anonymize video and sensor data before transfer, reducing bandwidth needs without sacrificing essential signals.
review: Trade-off: broader data access improves collaboration but increases governance complexity; gap: there is no explicit mechanism for cross-institution data retention policies or time-bound access rights.

name: Governance integration and external advisory engagement
consequences: Formalized governance structures with external advisory support can improve oversight and methodological alignment, but add coordination overhead and potential delays in decision-making. This can slow rapid iterations if advisory feedback cycles are not tightly managed downstream.
options: Establish a rotating external scientific advisory board with quarterly milestones and structured progress reviews to align on study ethics and methods.
Create parallel ethics and regulatory workstreams to streamline approvals and reduce rework when protocol amendments occur.
Pilot collaborative projects with regional sleep centers to validate methods on independent cohorts while preserving core data governance.
review: Trade-off: enhanced oversight improves reliability but can slow operational agility; gap: without defined escalation paths, critical course corrections may be delayed.

name: Event-triage throughput and annotation load optimization
consequences: Improving throughput increases the number of adjudicated events per night while maintaining dual scoring standards, but may shift bias toward easier-to-score events; downstream, backlog could still occur if adjudication capacity is exceeded.
options: Develop a semi-automated event-triage workflow with a calibrated threshold to maximize adjudicated events per night while preserving dual scoring integrity.
Institute a stratified reviewer rotation and defined adjudication windows to reduce backlog and ensure consistent scoring across nights.
Implement active learning where each adjudicated event improves the scoring model for subsequent nights and informs scheduling priorities.
review: Trade-off: automation reduces manual load but may introduce bias toward easier-to-score events; gap: early-phase dataset may be too small to train robust models.

name: Recruitment stability and matched-control maintenance
consequences: Maintaining recruitment channels and matched-control enrollment is essential for consistent data yield and baseline comparability; variability in enrollment pace can delay aims and impact power for longitudinal analyses. Sustained recruitment also influences budget pacing and staff workload.
options: Maintain recruitment outreach within University Hospital Bonn and regional networks with strict eligibility checks to stabilize enrollment pace.
Implement rolling matched-control enrollment with staggered start times to ensure baseline comparability while maximizing uptime.
Offer structured participation incentives and schedule flexibility to boost retention and ensure data yield across weeks.
review: Trade-off: stable enrollment improves data continuity but increases costs; gap: risk of selection bias if incentives drive enrollment patterns without mitigation.
